_about: The Watch film's narration. Cue text is the exact caption; tools/narration/pronunciations.json only changes what is spoken. Each segment is one step of the journey (src/content/film.ts maps segments to steps, camera and process timing). Build with tools/narration/build.sh.

cues.text: This is a fab: a factory for computer chips.
Over the next few minutes, we'll follow one silicon wafer through it.
It starts as a bare, polished disc, and it ends as a working circuit: an inverter, the simplest logic gate, built from just two transistors.
Wafers travel between machines in sealed pods called FOUPs, twenty-five at a time.
The pod docks at a load port, and its door opens only inside the machine, so the wafers never meet the air of the room.
Ours is bare silicon, polished to a mirror.
A robot reaches in on a thin blade and lifts our wafer out.
On the pre-aligner, the wafer turns until a sensor finds a small notch in its edge.
From now on, every machine knows exactly which way it is facing.
Before anything is built, a laser sweeps the surface.
A speck of dust scatters light into a detector, and each one becomes a dot on a defect map.
Particles far smaller than a hair can still ruin a circuit.
So the wafer is cleaned: chemicals and ultrapure water spray across it as it spins, lifting particles away.
Anything left now would be buried under the layers to come.
The wafer will carry hundreds of identical chips, called dies, laid out in a grid.
We'll follow this one.
Every pattern is printed across the whole wafer, one exposure field at a time.
Now the building begins.
In a furnace, oxygen reacts with the hot silicon and grows a thin skin of silicon dioxide, partly consuming the silicon beneath.
Then a layer of silicon nitride is deposited on top. Together, they form a hard mask for what comes next.
The first pattern marks out islands where the transistors will live.
That takes lithography, which we'll see in full shortly.
Then a plasma etch cuts trenches through the nitride and deep into the silicon around each island.
The trenches are filled with oxide.
Then the wafer is polished flat, down to the nitride, and the nitride is stripped away.
Each silicon island now sits in its own insulating moat, so neighbouring transistors can't leak into each other.
Next, the silicon is prepared for two kinds of transistor.
Resist covers one half, while an implanter fires phosphorus ions into the other.
Then the masks swap, and boron goes into the second half.
Nothing looks different, but the silicon now conducts in two different ways.
A short trip back to the furnace.
Heat lets the implanted atoms settle into the crystal, where they become electrically active, and it repairs the damage the ions left behind.
Now the most delicate layer: the gate oxide, only a few nanometres thick.
On top of it goes a film of polysilicon.
Once patterned, it becomes the gates: the switches that turn each transistor on and off.
Here is lithography in full.
In the track, the wafer is baked dry and primed with a vapour that helps the resist stick.
A nozzle pours a puddle of photoresist onto the centre.
The wafer spins up, the resist spreads into a thin, even film, and the excess flies off the edge.
A fine jet of solvent cleans the rim.
A hot plate drives most of the solvent out of the resist, leaving a firm, stable film.
Meanwhile, the scanner loads the reticle for this layer.
It is a quartz plate carrying the pattern in chrome, drawn four times larger than it will print.
Before exposing, the scanner finds alignment marks left by the first pattern.
It adjusts its stages so the gates will land exactly on the islands.
Deep ultraviolet light, at 193 nanometres, passes through the reticle.
The lens shrinks the image four times, and the scanner sweeps it across the wafer, field by field.
Where the light strikes, the resist changes chemically. Nothing can be seen yet: this is a latent image.
A second bake lets that chemistry finish, turning the exposed resist soluble.
Then the developer.
This is a positive resist, so wherever the light fell, the resist dissolves and washes away.
What remains are resist lines, exactly where the chrome cast its shadow.
An electron microscope measures the lines.
If they're out of specification, the resist can still be stripped and the whole cycle repeated.
After the next step, there's no going back.
In the etch chamber, a plasma sends ions straight down onto the wafer.
They carve through the polysilicon wherever it's uncovered, and stop at the thin gate oxide.
The resist lines have become polysilicon gates.
An oxygen plasma burns away the leftover resist.
That was one complete lithography cycle. Every patterned layer of a chip goes through the same loop, each with its own reticle.
The loop runs twice more, to implant the sources and drains: arsenic for one transistor, boron for the other.
The gates themselves block the ions, so every source and drain lines up perfectly with its gate.
Our two transistors are complete.
Now they must be wired together.
First, a thick layer of insulating oxide buries them, polished perfectly flat.
Another coat of resist, and the contact reticle is aligned to the gates beneath.
If it drifts too far, a contact could land on the wrong terminal.
The contact holes are printed into the resist, and their position is checked before anything is etched.
Then the plasma cuts narrow holes down through the oxide, stopping on the silicon and polysilicon below.
Tungsten fills the holes.
Polishing removes everything above the oxide, leaving a metal plug in each one.
The first level of copper wiring is built the same way.
Trenches are etched into a fresh insulating layer, filled with copper and polished flat.
These wires join the two transistors into one circuit, and bring in power and ground.
A second level goes on top, connected to the first through small vias.
Real chips stack many more levels; our inverter needs just two.
Finally, a tough passivation layer seals the chip against moisture and scratches, with windows left open over the pads.
The finished wafer is scanned one last time, and the results of every inspection along the way are reviewed together.
Now the test. A probe card touches the pads of each die in turn, and runs the inverter through its paces.
Each result is marked on the wafer map.
The wafer is mounted on tape, and sawn along the narrow streets between the dies.
A good die is picked from the tape and bonded into a package.
Gold wires, finer than a hair, link its pads to the package leads.
Then the whole assembly is sealed in epoxy.
And here is our inverter.
With the input low, the PMOS transistor conducts, and the output goes high.
With the input high, the NMOS transistor takes over, and the output goes low.
A working logic gate: one of the building blocks of every digital chip.
That's the journey: one wafer, dozens of steps, and one idea repeated again and again.
Lithography draws a pattern in light, and every other process makes it permanent.
A modern chip repeats that loop dozens of times, to build billions of transistors.
